title: The 1953 press and radio promotion group
summary: Reading a 1953 Courier item, Tex describes a short-lived group of writers and DJs who tried to promote New Orleans music jointly, and recalls local athletes.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: This is also from the Pittsburgh Courier. This is about that. It's from November 7, 1953 of the Pittsburgh Courier. And so maybe you could read it. It's just a little article.

The Chicago Press and Radio Men and Public Relations representative from several fronts met on that Wednesday in the home of James Okidoki Smith down on St. Anthony Street. And we elected Johnny Russo, editor of the Courier, Louisiana Dish and President, along with Elgin Hichu of the Louisiana Weekly as vice president. Now, Elgin Hichu was born in Houston, Texas, and he died in Houston, Texas. He died of diabetes. And when he left the Louisiana Weekly, he went back to Houston, Texas. And I understand one of his relatives left him a big recording studio, and he started recording music. I'm trying to think of the name of the organization that he set up there in Houston, Texas. But we put this thing together in order to do promotions for the city of New Orleans as far as music, information on radio, information on television, or just whatever. And I was in the middle of it with Okidoki, Earl Woodbury, who at that time was the owner of Club Valley, and Oynes Butch Curry, who was working for the Courier at the time. That's Curry, not the Courier. His name is C-U-R-R-Y. The Courier was C-U-R-I-E-R. So this is, now we put this thing together to do these kind of promotions, and whatever advertising that was going to be done, all of us wanted to try to share in it in order to promote either the radio station or the various newspapers. But we were trying to do it collectively. It only lasted for a short while. It didn't, it really didn't bloom or blossom the way it really should have done, because lack of time on us working for other companies, lack of money, and things like that. Well, like I said, there are many factors that stopped us from doing what we really should have done. And a lot of this was aired on old WMRY back in 1953. So when I think about, I think about my good friend Gully Carter, who also was a very, very good friend. And then, you know, as I look at many of the things here, I'm looking at the names here on this sheet. Like I said, Louis White, who was one of the outstanding young basketball players who played at Corpus Christi Church Auditorium. And that's when they had this CYO, these Catholic youth organizations. And Louis wound up becoming a furniture salesman. And he's still alive today. I hadn't seen him for quite a while. And I think about Al Parker, who was an outstanding football player back at Xavier University during his day, who was an outstanding football player and a very good athlete. You know, New Orleans gave birth to the first black, wait a minute, the first black independent football league right here in the city of New Orleans. They had the Brutes and the Hawks, the Southsiders, the Trojans. Let me see. I hope I'm not leaving anybody out. Well, and my brother-in-law, Al Piku, who played for the Trojans, was an outstanding running back. I'm just thinking today, if he was about 19, 20 years of age, he'd probably be in pro football today because he was just that dynamic. When I think about Oliver Thompson, who was a classmate of mine at night down to 35, was an outstanding football player. So we used to call him Tiny Thompson. He was small in stature, about five feet, six inches tall. And he was probably one of the fastest men ever come out of New Orleans. The reason why he was so fast, by being small, he had to learn how to run fast. So nobody could catch up with him.
